t: 3183. The Number of Ways to Make the Sum
o: Count multisets of coins summing to n, where coins 1, 2, 6 are unlimited but coin 4 may be used at most twice. Order does not matter. For n=4 the ways are [1,1,1,1], [1,1,2], [2,2], [4] — note [4] uses one 4 and [2,2] uses none. With n up to 1e5, a knapsack-style DP over sums is the intended tool.
k: Process coin types one at a time so each combination is counted exactly once (order-independent).
Unbounded coins use a forward (ascending) loop; the bounded coin 4 contributes dp[s-4] + dp[s-8] in a snapshot-based pass.
Doing two independent 0/1 passes for coin 4 double-counts single-4 combinations — use a snapshot of dp instead.

a.i: Let dp[s] be the number of ways to form sum s using the coin types processed so far. Coins 1 and 2 are unbounded, so a classic ascending-loop update suffices. Coin 4 is capped at two copies: capture a snapshot of dp and set dp[s] += snap[s-4] + snap[s-8], which counts using zero, one, or two 4s exactly once each. Finally add coin 6 as unbounded. Processing types sequentially guarantees each multiset is counted once.
s: Run unbounded updates for coins 1 and 2 (ascending sums).
Snapshot dp; for each s add snap[s-4] and, if s >= 8, snap[s-8].
Run an unbounded update for coin 6 and return dp[n] modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n) — a constant number of linear passes over sums
a.sp: O(n) for the DP array and its snapshot

w: Sanity checks: n=4 gives 4 and n=12 gives 22, matching the examples. The classic pitfall is the bounded coin: two sequential 0/1 passes wrongly allow reusing the snapshot and double-count. A follow-up could generalize to arbitrary per-coin caps, solved with the bounded-knapsack sliding-window technique per residue class.
